Collision Domain and Broadcast Domain
Definitions
A collision domain is a network region in which simultaneous
transmissions can interfere.
A broadcast domain is a group of interfaces that receives a Layer-2
broadcast.
Hub example
Four devices on one hub
Collision domains : one shared
Broadcast domains : one
Switch with one VLAN
Four devices on four ports
Each link is separate
All ports share one VLAN
broadcast domain
Switch with three VLANs
VLAN 10 Broadcast domain 1
VLAN 20 Broadcast domain 2
VLAN 30 Broadcast domain 3
Arrangement Collisions Broadcast scope
Shared hub
Shared domain
One domain
Switched full duplex
Separate links
One domain per
VLAN
Switch, three VLANs
Separate links
Three domains
Key takeaway: Switching separates shared collision conditions.
VLANs divide the network into separate Layer-2 broadcast
domains.
Why Ethernet Uses Frames
Problem
The physical layer transfers signals and bits. The receiver needs a
defined structure to interpret the incoming information.
An Ethernet frame provides
•A recognisable start
•Destination and source identification
•Payload-type information
•A location for upper-layer data
•Minimum-size support
•Error-detection information

Processing flow at the receiver
1Check destination MAC
Should this frame be processed? Only if it is for 00:10:20:30:40:50.

The receiver hands the payload to IPv4 processing.
Interpretation: every field answers one question

Minimum Frame Size and Padding
For an untagged frame, the 64-byte minimum runs from destination MAC through FCS
Dest MAC
6 B
Src MAC
6 B
Type
2 B Actual data
20 B
Padding
26 B
FCS
4 B
Header 14 B Payload area = 46 bytes (data + padding) FCS 4 B
1. Fixed overhead
Destination MAC 6 bytes
Source MAC 6 bytes
Type / EtherType 2 bytes
FCS 4 bytes
These four fields are always present, whatever the payload
looks like.
Total fixed = 18 bytes
2. Required payload area
Minimum frame 64 bytes
Less fixed fields 18 bytes
Min payload + pad 46 bytes
Untagged payload plus padding must occupy at least 46
bytes. Pad shorter data.
64 - 18 = 46 bytes
3. Worked example
Required payload area 46 bytes
Actual upper-layer data 20 bytes
Required padding 26 bytes
6 + 6 + 2 + 20 + 26 + 4 64 bytes
With only 20 bytes of data, 26 bytes of padding bring the
frame back up to 64 bytes.
Padding = 46 - 20 = 26 bytes
For untagged frames, padding brings payloads under 46 bytes up to the 64-byte minimum frame size.
Frame Size Worked Examples
Untagged frame length: 18 bytes of header and trailer + at least 46 bytes of data and padding
Data arrives from the upper layer Is the data smaller than 46 bytes? Yes - pad up to 46 B / No - pad 0 B Frame = 6 + 6 + 2 + payload area + 4
Example 1: 10-byte data
6 B 6 B 2 B 10 36 pad 4 B
Minimum payload area = 46 bytes
Actual data = 10 bytes
Padding required = 36 bytes
Frame = 6+6+2+10+36+4 = 64 bytes
Example 2: 46-byte data
6 B 6 B 2 B 46 data 4 B
Minimum payload area = 46 bytes
Actual data = 46 bytes
Padding required = 0 bytes
Frame = 6+6+2+46+4 = 64 bytes
Example 3: 100-byte data
6 B 6 B 2 B 100 data 4 B
Data exceeds the 46-byte minimum
No padding is added
Padding required = 0 bytes
Frame = 6+6+2+100+4 = 118 bytes
Important note: do not add the 8-byte preamble and SFD when calculating the conventional 64-to-1518-byte frame length.
For link utilisation, however, every frame also costs 8 bytes of preamble/SFD plus a 96-bit-time interframe gap (12 byte times) - about 20 bytes of overhead per frame.
Key takeaway: an untagged frame needs padding when its data is shorter than 46 bytes.
Frame Check Sequence
Purpose - the Frame Check Sequence lets the receiver detect whether the frame was corrupted during transmission.
Sender operation
Frame information
Header and payload are assembled.
CRC calculation
CRC-32 covers destination MAC through
payload and padding.
FCS appended to the frame
The CRC result becomes the 4-byte FCS
field.
Frame transmitted
The frame leaves the interface onto the
wire.
Receiver operation
Frame received - CRC recalculated
The receiver repeats the same check over the frame.
Compared with the received FCS
Recalculated value is matched against the appended
FCS.
Match
No error detected by
FCS. Continue
processing.
No match
Frame error detected -
the frame is discarded.
What the FCS does - and does not
What the FCS does
Detects most, but not all, transmission
corruption
Lets the receiver identify an invalid frame
What the FCS does not do
Does not correct damaged bits
Does not guarantee retransmission or
delivery
Does not replace higher-layer reliability
FCS detects errors, without guaranteeing delivery. CRC includes any VLAN tag but excludes preamble, SFD and the FCS itself.

Question 1
What is the minimum conventional untagged frame size, destination
MAC through FCS?
A. 18 bytes
B. 46 bytes
C. 64 bytes
D. 1518 bytes
Question 2
An untagged frame carries 30 bytes of data. How much padding is
required?
A. 0 bytes
B. 16 bytes
C. 30 bytes
D. 46 bytes
Question 3
Which field identifies the protocol carried in the payload?
A. Destination MAC
B. EtherType
C. Preamble
D. FCS
Question 4
Which field detects that a frame has been corrupted?
A. Source MAC
B. Payload
C. FCS
D. SFD
Answers
1. C 2. B 3. B 4. C
Explanation
•The 64-byte minimum is measured from the destination MAC through the FCS
•For this untagged frame: padding = 46 - 30 = 16 bytes
•EtherType names the protocol carried inside the payload
•The FCS is a CRC that detects a corrupted frame
